how-to-bid-tree-removal.html.text:
TREE SERVICE ESTIMATING

How to bid tree removal without guessing the day rate

Homeowners type “tree removal cost” and see $200–$2,000. That range is not a market. It is what happens when a 12-inch street pine and a 36-inch backyard oak get priced with the same rule. If you run a crew, the job is to bid the stop you are actually going to work — not the average of someone else’s internet answers.

Use the free tree service bid calculator to run the arithmetic. This page is the method behind it.

Wood volume scales with DBH squared

Diameter at breast height is the one measurement every estimator already takes. The mistake is treating it as linear. Trunk volume — and the climbing, rigging, and chipping that ride with it — grows closer to the square of diameter. A 24-inch tree is about four times the wood of a 12-inch tree of the same height, not twice. A flat “$25 an inch” quote underprices the oak that takes the afternoon and overprices the ornamental you could have finished before lunch.

Height matters, but less than people think once the tree is past a story or two. A 40-foot and a 70-foot tree of the same DBH are not the same job, and they are also not twice as different as the diameters. Species is a modifier (hardwood is denser and slower; palm is a different job), not the main event.

Access and targets change the hours more than species

The same 18-inch maple is a different bid on the driveway than it is over a ranch roof with the chipper on the street. Carry distance, a fence you cannot drop, and a target you have to rig away from all add hours without adding wood. Power lines are not a percentage you invent on the hood of the truck — they are either in the bid, a utility hold, or a walk-away.

A crane day is a real cost. Charge it once for the stop if any tree needs it, not as a vague “hard access” bump that disappears when the homeowner asks you to sharpen the pencil.

The four lines that eat the margin

  1. Stump grinding. Often quoted as an afterthought, then done anyway. Price it from stump diameter, not as “another $100.”
  2. Haul and dump. Leaving firewood, chipping on site, and hauling logs are three different jobs. Dump tickets are not overhead; they are this stop.
  3. Travel. The whole crew and the chipper are on the clock for the drive. Bill travel once for the stop, not once per tree.
  4. Payroll burden. A climber at $35 is not a $35 hour. Workers’ compensation in this trade is expensive. If you price off the raw wage, you are short before you start.

A mobilization minimum protects the 20-minute drive for a 6-inch ornamental. If the priced job is under that floor, the quote is the floor.

The two numbers to hold when they ask you to come down

Walk-away is total cost — labor, equipment, dump, overhead. Below that the job makes nothing. Price per inch of total DBH is the sanity check against last month’s work. If a stop comes out at $12 an inch on hard access, the hours or the fees are wrong. If it comes out at $90 an inch on a street pine, you are about to lose the job to someone who actually timed it.

What this is not

This is not a tree appraisal, a hazard rating, or advice to remove a tree. It is not a wage determination. It does not replace walking the site, checking for utilities, or knowing your own crew. The calculator is arithmetic on numbers you type. You remain the estimator.

Open the calculator and price a stop

Common questions

How do tree services price a removal?

Most profitable crews bid time and materials from diameter at breast height, height, species, access, and targets — not a flat per-inch rule and not a day-rate guess. Wood volume scales with the square of DBH, so a 24-inch tree is about four times the wood of a 12-inch tree of the same height.

Why is a per-inch tree removal price misleading?

A linear per-inch price underprices the big tree and overprices the small one. Hours grow closer to DBH squared because that is how trunk volume grows. Access, power lines, and a backyard carry then change the hours more than species does.

What do tree services forget to include in a bid?

Stump grinding, haul and dump fees, the drive for the whole crew and chipper, payroll burden, and a mobilization minimum on small ornamental trees. Those five lines are how a quote that looked fine loses money.

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice. Verify every figure against your own costs and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid.

FOR TREE SERVICE OWNERS

Bid the tree, the access, and the wood.

A 24-inch backyard oak is four times the wood of a 12-inch street pine — not twice. Price a removal stop from diameter, height, species, access, targets, stump grinding, and haul, then add the drive, the loaded crew, and the margin you intend to keep. You get the bid, the walk-away number, and which tree is actually carrying the job.

How tree services actually bid a removal

This calculator vs. SingleOps

This calculator vs. a flat per-inch rate

The stop

One row per tree. Hours grow with the square of DBH because that is how wood volume grows. Access and targets change the hours more than species does.

Your costs

Crew hourly is what you pay the whole crew for an hour on the clock — climber, ground, and chipper operator together. Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation (expensive in this trade), and insurance. Travel is billed once for the stop, not once per tree. A crane day is charged only if any tree is marked crane-required.

A bid link carries the whole stop — every tree, access, and your rates — so the page reopens exactly as you left it. Send it to yourself or your crew. The customer should get the price, not the link.

Which tree is carrying the job

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The hour factors are starting points, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee — time your own crews and replace the wages and fees with yours.

    Common questions

    Why not just quote a price per inch of trunk diameter?

    Because wood volume does not grow with diameter, it grows with diameter squared. This tool uses (DBH ÷ 12)² against a 12-inch reference tree, so a 24" trunk is four times the wood of a 12" one at the same height — not twice. A linear per-inch rule underprices every big removal on the schedule and overprices the small ones, which is how a crew stays busy all season and still finishes the year flat.

    What actually drives the hours — species or access?

    Access, usually by a wide margin. Species moves the base hours by a factor of 0.7 (palm) to 1.25 (oak, maple, hickory, beech), with mixed or unknown at 1.0. Access moves them from 1.0 at the street with the chipper at the tree, to 1.15 for a side yard, 1.4 for carrying brush out of a backyard, 1.75 for a tight backyard or work over a structure, and 2.1 when a crane is required. Hazard premiums stack on top of that and add up: +25% near a structure, +40% near power, +20% for a dead or hazardous tree. Those are pricing factors for your own estimate, not a hazard rating or a recommendation to remove anything — that is an arborist's call.

    How is haul priced separately from the removal?

    As a share of the tree's base removal hours, before access and hazard multipliers: leaving wood on site is 0, chipping on site and leaving the chips is 0.12, chip-and-haul is 0.35, and hauling logs is 0.45. The two haul options that actually leave the property also add a dump fee per tree. Basing haul on base hours rather than the multiplied figure keeps a backyard carry from being counted twice — the carry is already in the access multiplier.

    Does the stump grind come out of the removal price?

    No, it is its own line and only when you tick it. Grind hours are about 0.2 h of setup plus a growth term that scales with the stump's face — diameter squared, not diameter, because the wheel sweeps the whole cross-section — roughly 0.6 h for a 12" stump and 3.8 h for a 36" one (three times the diameter is nine times the face), in the range a two-person grind crew actually spends including repositioning. You can enter a stump diameter that differs from DBH, which is what you want on a flared or previously topped tree.

    Why does a one-small-tree job come out at the minimum charge?

    Because a stop costs more than its cutting. Round-trip drive for the whole crew is priced from the travel minutes you enter and billed at the loaded crew rate, equipment is charged per on-site hour, and a crane — if any tree on the stop needs one — is a day rate charged once for the whole stop, not per tree. When the margin price still lands under your mobilization floor, the floor is used instead and the result says so. That is the number a "can you just take out this little one?" call actually costs you.

    Is my bid data uploaded anywhere?

    No. No account and no network requests — the address, the trees, your wages, and your prices stay in this browser. The stop itself saves to this browser's local storage as you type, so it is still here on your next visit, and "Start a fresh bid" clears it. "Copy bid link" puts the same numbers in a URL you can send yourself or your crew instead — treat a copied link like your rate sheet, since it carries every tree and rate. The business details saved for the printed proposal live in this browser's local storage separately, and "Forget my business details" clears them. The optional local usage counter records only which features were used and the day, and the footer checkbox turns it off.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

vs-a-flat-per-inch-rate.html.text:
← Tree Service Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-inch rate

“$X a diameter inch, any tree” is not a price for a removal — it is a price for one tree's size, access, and hazards, quietly applied to a tree twice the diameter and four times the trouble.

What a flat per-inch rate is

A flat per-inch rate is the fastest way to quote a removal over the phone: multiply the trunk diameter by a number and read it back. Customers like it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it was usually set for one kind of tree — a small-to-mid street tree the chipper can reach directly — and then reused for every tree afterward, whether or not the next one is twice the diameter, tucked in a backyard, growing next to the house, or has a stump to grind.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each tree's DBH, height, species, access, haul method, stump grinding, and hazard flags (near a structure, near power, dead), plus your own crew rate, payroll burden, equipment cost, overhead, and target margin. It converts DBH to a size factor using the square of diameter, applies species, height, access, and hazard multipliers, and returns the price, the price per inch, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price — for this tree, not a flat rate for every tree.

What a flat per-inch rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges twice as much for a tree twice the diameter, even though a tree twice the diameter has roughly four times the wood volume and rigging complexity. Converts DBH to a size factor using the square of diameter (the same shape a grinder wheel or a climber actually faces), so hours scale with volume, not inches.
Charges the same whether the chipper sits right at the tree or the crew has to carry every branch out of a tight backyard. Applies an access multiplier — street, side yard, backyard, tight backyard, or crane required — on top of the size factor.
Has no line for a tree next to a structure, near a power line, or standing dead, even though each of those changes how carefully (and slowly) the crew has to work. Applies a hazard premium per flag — near-structure, near-power, dead — stacked on top of the base removal hours.
Has no line for grinding the stump or for chipping and hauling versus leaving the wood on site. Prices stump grinding by stump face area and haul method by its own share of on-site hours, separate from the removal itself.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price, the price per inch, and the effective hourly rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two trees, one flat rate

Using this calculator's own defaults for crew rate, burden, equipment, overhead, and target margin:

A 12-inch street pine, softwood, chipper right at the tree, wood left on site, costs $397.58 to run and this calculator prices it at $530.10 — $44.18 per inch. A 24-inch backyard oak — hardwood, next to the house, wood chipped and hauled, stump ground — costs $4,897.39 to run and this calculator prices it at $6,529.85, 12.32 times the pine's price on just twice the diameter. Quote the oak at the pine's flat $44.18-per-inch rate instead, and 24 inches prices at $1,060.21 — $3,837.18 below the oak's own break-even cost — before counting the $5,469.65 it falls short of what this calculator prices the oak at. Same rate, one tree that pays and one that loses money the moment the ladder goes up against the house.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-inch rate get a bigger tree wrong?

Because wood volume, and the climbing and rigging complexity that rides with it, scales with the square of diameter at breast height, not linearly with inches. Using this calculator's own defaults, a 12-inch street pine costs $397.58 to run and this calculator prices it at $530.10 -- $44.18 per inch. A 24-inch backyard oak next to the house, needing a stump grind and a chip-and-haul, costs $4,897.39 to run and this calculator prices it at $6,529.85 -- 12.32 times the pine's price, on twice the diameter.

What does a flat per-inch rate usually leave out entirely?

Access, hazards, stump grinding, and haul. A flat per-inch number has no line for a backyard the crew has to carry brush out of instead of chipping at the tree, no line for a tree next to a structure or power line, no line for grinding the stump, and no line for chipping and hauling versus leaving the wood on site. It also assumes wood volume scales with inches instead of the square of inches, which is wrong on every tree above the size the rate was set on.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own defaults: the 12-inch street pine prices at $530.10, on a job that costs $397.58 to run, at a $44.18-per-inch rate. Apply that same per-inch rate to the 24-inch backyard oak and it quotes at $1,060.21 -- $3,837.18 below the oak's own $4,897.39 break-even cost, before counting the $5,469.65 it falls short of what this calculator prices the oak at ($6,529.85, 12.32 times the pine).

Is a flat per-inch rate ever the right way to quote?

For trees close to the size, species, and access the rate was set on -- typically a small-to-mid street tree with the chipper right there -- a flat per-inch number can land close, because that is probably the tree the rate was set on. The risk is quoting a much larger tree, a hard-access backyard removal, or a tree with hazards or a stump to grind at the same rate, because the rate does not know the diameter squared, the access, or the hazards until someone looks at the tree, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted over the phone.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or dump fees?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your dump facility's fees, or what other tree services in your area charge. It takes DBH, height, species, access, haul method, stump grinding, hazard flags, and your own crew rate, burden, equipment cost, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this tree -- the arithmetic a flat per-inch rate skips, not a market survey.

Open the Tree Service Bid Calculator to price your own removal, or read how tree services actually bid a removal.

← Tree Service Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. SingleOps

Two different shapes: SingleOps is an account-based platform for running a tree-care or landscape company's whole operation, including scheduling and invoicing a job once it is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this removal stop cost, before you offer it to the customer.

What each tool is for

SingleOps is a business management platform built for tree care, landscaping and other green-industry service companies. It is used to run CRM and lead tracking, estimating and proposal generation, scheduling and crew routing, invoicing and payments, and QuickBooks integration across a whole operation, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. SingleOps's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that estimating and scheduling software describe building, tracking and billing a job once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a new removal stop should cost from tree-by-tree wood volume, access, haul and crew cost before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what SingleOps does. It does not track a lead, schedule a crew across a season, or invoice a customer. It takes one stop's trees — each one's diameter, height, species, access, targets and haul choice — plus stump grinding, travel, loaded crew cost, equipment, a crane day if one tree needs it, overhead and target margin, and turns that into the recommended stop price, the walk-away floor, the price per inch of DBH, the effective crew hourly rate, and which tree on the stop is actually carrying the job — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears your own break-even floor, and a printable customer proposal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to track leads, schedule crews, and invoice customers for tree and landscape jobs across my whole business.SingleOps, or a comparable green-industry platform — running that ongoing operation is not something this calculator does.

Which tree on a multi-tree stop is actually carrying the price, before I decide whether to discount one of them?This calculator's per-tree hour and price split.
A customer's budget is below what I'd normally quote. Does it still clear my walk-away floor?This calculator's proposed-price check — it flags a price below break-even before you agree to it.
I already have stops priced and need to schedule, invoice and track them across many customers, over a season.SingleOps — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a per-tree removal price actually work?This calculator's own bidding walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. SingleOps's tools are used through a paid account.

Most tree services get different value from each: SingleOps (or a comparable green-industry platform) for running leads, crews and invoicing across an ongoing business as an account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what a new removal stop should cost before it is offered. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a signed proposal, an invoice, or an arborist's hazard assessment.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or SingleOps?

They do different jobs, and a tree-care business of any size will likely end up touching both.
